summary:
Egypt presents a direct and documented entry risk to trans visitors. The Ministry of Interior holds broad powers under the immigration law to refuse entry to, or deport, anyone whose presence is said to disturb public order and morality, and those powers have been applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Cairo 52 study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) analyses that law and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents between 2018 and 2022. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights separately records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even where no charge is ever upheld. Removal therefore does not require any offence under Egyptian law.

Same-sex conduct is not expressly written into the penal statutes, but prosecutions are a routine outcome rather than a theoretical one. Economic Courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, and the resulting sentences are custodial. Court of Cassation interpretations from the 1970s had already removed the requirement of a financial exchange, so habitual conduct or multiple partners is sufficient to ground a charge.

Police obtain that evidence through entrapment. A BBC investigation, "How Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps", documents officers running fake profiles on dating applications, with victims describing blackmail and arrest; the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records the same pattern and notes that transgender women are a particular target. Arrests are obtained without any explicit prohibition on homosexuality being invoked.

Arrest carries physical risk. Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing documents rising arrests of gay and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations, and reports that authorities turn a blind eye; the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records continuing violations inside police stations. There is no anti-discrimination law or policy covering sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, so none of this conduct is met by a statutory protection.

Legal gender recognition is being actively closed. A Ministry of Interior directive issued to civil-registry heads nationwide in December 2024 shuts the loophole in Civil Status Law 143/1994 that had allowed transgender Egyptians to correct their gender marker through governorate committees.

Healthcare is a further documented barrier. TIMEP's 6 January 2025 submission for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle states that transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health, with barriers to equitable services persisting since the previous cycle and pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare settings.

Expression is constrained as well as conduct. Morality and public-order provisions criminalise "any behavior, or the expression of any idea" deemed immoral or offensive to religious teachings, giving police wide discretion over LGBTQ expression. The Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order in 2017 barring "the appearance of the homosexuals" or "promoting their slogans" in media, and legislation introduced in August 2018 places any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws.

Marriage and partnership offer no protection. Personal and family law follows the religious law of the person's recognised religion, none of which recognises same-sex relationships, so Egyptian law recognises marriage only between a man and a woman. If a same-sex relationship becomes public, police may use it as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.
tangentialFactors:
The current enforcement pattern rests on a longer history of state action against LGBTQ people. Human Rights Watch, in "In a Time of Torture" (29 February 2004), documented the Queen Boat-era crackdown, including arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings inflicted over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants. The September 2017 rainbow flag incident produced a comparable wave: at least 84 arrests between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many of those detained subjected to forced anal tests, and a state of trauma and despair among young Egyptian LGBTQ individuals with numerous attempted suicides. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after that incident, fled abroad, was granted asylum and died by suicide in 2020.

Media figures have driven prosecutions and incitement. After the 2017 flag incident, TV hosts Ahmed Moussa and Mohamed Al Gheity repeatedly incited violence against the community, and Moussa published personal information of flag-raisers. In December 2014 TV presenter Mona Iraqi collaborated with police to raid a public bathhouse, arresting around 26 men, who were later acquitted. In January 2019 host Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his television show. In 2009 the newspaper Al Balagh Al Gadid was shut down and two reporters jailed for printing a story about actors' involvement in homosexual prostitution. In 2013 comedian Bassem Youssef was charged by the Morsi government with "propagating and promoting homosexuality and obscenity".

Social environment compounds legal risk. Pew Research Center found that 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and polling suggests only a minority support LGBTQ rights, which is why Egyptian political parties and human rights NGOs do not express public support. The term "khawalat", historically male cross-dressing dancers, has been stigmatised and is used as a derogatory term for passive and gay men, and Egyptian cinema has portrayed queer characters almost exclusively through stereotyping and defamation. State officials and police are recorded as routinely harassing, abusing and torturing LGBTQ people, particularly trans people, leading to unfair arrests and abuse in custody.

Advocacy has not produced legal reform. After the 2011 revolution LGBTQ activists became more visible and online campaigns against homophobia and transphobia went viral on Twitter and Facebook by 2013, without any resulting change in the legal position. In August 2021 the Central Bank of Egypt confirmed that rainbow holograms on new banknotes were an anti-counterfeiting feature after online critics suggested they were covert LGBTQ support.
localsOnly:
Egyptian transgender people lost the administrative route to correcting a gender marker. The Civil Status Law 143/1994 had permitted corrections through governorate committees, and the Ministry of Interior directive of December 2024 instructs civil-registry heads nationwide to close that route, leaving residents without a domestic mechanism for legal gender recognition.

Residents face the same charging framework as visitors but without the option of departure. Economic Courts ground explicit criminalisation in Penal Code provisions read with Article 9(C) of Law 10/1961, and Court of Cassation reasoning from the 1970s means habitual conduct or multiple partners suffices without any financial exchange. Bedayaa records rising arrests of gay and trans Egyptians alongside coerced anal examinations, and the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records violations continuing inside police stations.

Transgender and intersex Egyptians encounter discrimination in healthcare. TIMEP's January 2025 UPR submission identifies discriminatory laws, policies and practices as violations of the right to health, with barriers to equitable services persisting since the last cycle and pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare provision.

No statutory protection exists for residents either. There is no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, and no anti-discrimination policy. Personal and family law follows the religious law of the person's recognised religion, so marriage is available only between a man and a woman, and a public same-sex relationship can be introduced as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality. Many Egyptian LGBTQ young people have left the country because of social and political threats.
outOfScopeNotes:
Several points remain unresolved in the sources available here. The December 2024 Ministry of Interior directive on civil-registry gender markers is reported by Cairo 52; whether it has been published in the official gazette, whether it is subject to challenge before the administrative courts, and whether any governorate has continued to process corrections after its issue are not established by the inventory.

No figure is available for the number of people prosecuted or convicted each year under the morality and debauchery provisions, nor for the number of foreign nationals deported on the grounds described. The 12 incidents analysed by Cairo 52 cover 2018 to 2022 and are documented cases, not a measure of total enforcement.

Whether coerced anal examinations continue after the reporting periods covered by Bedayaa and Human Rights Watch, and whether any official instruction prohibits them, is not sourced here. The current status of Egypt's UPR recommendations on the right to health for transgender and intersex people, referenced by TIMEP, is likewise not set out in the inventory.

A number of claims in this record rest on open-source country coverage rather than a primary legal instrument or a rights organisation's reporting, including the wording of the 2017 media order, the August 2018 social-network threshold, the 2013 and 2019 media prosecutions, the 2009 newspaper closure and the 2014 bathhouse raid. The underlying texts of the Penal Code articles and Article 9(C) of Law 10/1961 as applied by the Economic Courts are described secondhand and have not been read directly for this record.
